content: Hydrocephalus is a neurological condition characterized by the progressive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the intracranial space. This accumulation can result in increased intracranial pressure, ventricular enlargement (ventriculomegaly), and subsequent brain damage. The primary treatment for hydrocephalus involves the use of ventriculo-peritoneal shunt systems, which divert CSF to relieve pressure. However, there are various types of shunt systems available, and their effectiveness and safety profiles differ. The objective of this review was to compare the effectiveness and adverse effects of conventional shunt devices with more complex shunt systems for CSF diversion in individuals with hydrocephalus. The review included randomized controlled trials and quasi-randomized trials that evaluated different types of ventriculo-peritoneal shunting devices. The primary outcomes assessed were treatment failure, adverse events, and mortality. The review included six studies with a total of 962 participants. These studies compared standard valves to anti-syphon valves, other types of standard valves, self-adjusting CSF flow-regulating valves, and external differential programmable pressure valves. Most studies were conducted in hospital settings with follow-up in outpatient settings. The majority of participants were infants or children with hydrocephalus caused by various conditions. The certainty of the evidence for most comparisons was rated as low to very low. 1. Standard Valve vs. Anti-Syphon Valve Three studies with 296 participants compared standard valves to anti-syphon valves. The evidence regarding the incidence of treatment failure was very uncertain (very low certainty). Adverse events appeared to occur at similar rates in both groups, with ranges of 0–1.9% for standard valves and 0–2.9% for anti-syphon valves (low certainty). Mortality rates were also similar, with 0% for standard valves and 0.9% for anti-syphon valves (low certainty). Ventricular size and head circumference were comparable between the two groups (low certainty). None of the studies reported data on participants' quality of life. 2. Comparison Between Different Types of Standard Valves Two studies with 174 participants compared different types of standard valves. The evidence regarding treatment failure was very uncertain, with relative risks (RR) of 0.41 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.27) in the early postoperative period and 1.17 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.92) at 12 months (very low certainty). Adverse events were not reported separately from treatment failure. Mortality rates ranged from 2% to 17%, but the evidence was very uncertain (very low certainty). The studies did not report on quality of life, ventricular size reduction, or head circumference. 3. Standard Valve vs. Self-Adjusting CSF Flow-Regulating Valve One study with 229 participants compared standard valves to self-adjusting CSF flow-regulating valves. Treatment failure rates were similar, with 42.98% for standard valves and 39.13% for self-adjusting valves (low certainty). Adverse events were also comparable, with ranges of 0–1.9% for standard valves and 0–7.2% for self-adjusting valves (low certainty). No deaths were reported in the immediate postoperative period, but nine deaths occurred later, with no breakdown of data by intervention type (low certainty). The study did not report on quality of life, ventricular size reduction, or head circumference. 4. External Differential Programmable Pressure Valve vs. Non-Programmable Valve One study with 377 participants compared programmable valves to non-programmable valves. Treatment failure rates were similar, with 52% for both groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.24, low certainty). Adverse event rates were also comparable, with 6.19% for programmable valves and 6.01% for non-programmable valves (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.15, low certainty). The study did not report on mortality, quality of life, or head circumference. Ventricular size reduction was similar between the two groups (low certainty). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that standard shunt valves, anti-syphon valves, self-adjusting CSF flow-regulating valves, and external differential programmable pressure valves may have similar outcomes in terms of treatment failure, adverse events, and mortality. However, the certainty of the evidence is low to very low, and the review did not include valves with the latest technological advancements. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate newer valve technologies and to focus on patient-centered outcomes, including cost-effectiveness.
